# ParaScript

> A language model writes language well and does not reliably produce a spatially arranged solid from a prompt. It describes the solid in ParaScript. The workspace turns that script into the solid.

Read the language reference before writing a script. It begins with "Guidance for a language model". The compiler accepts only the forms that page describes. There is no upload API: a person pastes the finished script into the workspace and presses Run solver.

Write a shape once and call it wherever that shape appears, including at `export`. Do not copy its faces. Name each face for the surface it is. A cylinder is one `Tube` and two `Disk` calls. `Tube` and `Disk` are 2D faces. `Cylinder` is the solid that calls them. The broom's handle, ferrule, and hanging hole are three calls to one `Cylinder`, and `join` turns the hole.

Build a patterned part in this order. Bind `pi` when a curve needs it. That is a value the whole script shares. A size is a parameter of the part that uses it. The file writes those numbers once, in `parameters`. Read a parameter with `$`. `cut_holes` reads `$holes` and `add_pins` reads `$pins`. Bind `patterned_plate` as `cut_holes >> add_pins`, then export `patterned_plate(plate: Plate(size: $plate.size, thickness: $plate.thickness))`. `plate.origin` is an anchor on the solid. Write the primitive, then the base part. A plate is a square box: `Plate` calls `Box(width: size, depth: size, height: thickness)`. That box is centered on X and Y and stands on z = 0. The base part exposes the anchors a pattern reads, such as `origin` and `top`. `rectangular_pattern` returns the grid of points. `circular_pattern` returns the points of a circle. Both are `snake_case`. A component uses `PascalCase`, such as `Plate` and `CylinderAt`. Map `CylinderAt` over the points. The function receives the point and chooses `radius` and `height`, so each location can build its own cylinder. `CylinderAt` publishes `at`. `subtract_cylinders` cuts that list out of the plate. `add_cylinders` unions a list onto the plate. Read `plate.origin` and `plate.top`. The component at that call must expose every anchor you read. `map` and `filter` are built in. `|>` pipes a value into a function's next argument, and `>>` composes two functions and binds more tightly. `items |> map(f: item => ...)` fills `list`. `items |> map` is rejected. `integers(start: 0.0, count: 5.0)` is `[0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]`. `start` is the first whole number and `count` is how many. A list has no length, so the index list is an argument and has one entry per count. `map`'s parameter is named `item`. `filter`'s predicate returns the literal `true` or `false`.

A `def` may declare a signature. `def same: T => T => number` uses the type variable `T` for both parameters and returns a number. A repeated name is the same variable. `number`, `vector`, `boolean`, `string`, `component`, `solid`, `surface`, and `coordinate_system` are concrete types. `[T]` is a list of `T`. A tuple is `(1.0, true)`, and `(number, vector)` is its type. Each place keeps its own type. Take it apart with `let (n, point) = pair in`. There is no `pair.0`. A vector is `Vector(coords: coords, x:, y:, z:)`. `coords` comes from `Component`, which passes one coordinate system into `solid: coords =>` and `expose: coords =>`. A script cannot construct a coordinate system. A helper defined outside those callbacks takes `coords` and the call passes it, as in `Disk(coords: coords, radius: radius, z: 0.0)`. `join`'s last parameter is that coordinate system, and `join` ignores it, so pass `solid: join(...)`. A component does not expose that system. A direction a mate needs is an anchor. Inside `using`, move a point with `frame.top.offset(x:, y:, z:)`. Combine two vectors with `add(vector:)` or `subtract(vector:)`. Both must carry the same coordinate system, and the result keeps the receiver's system. `+` and `-` do not combine vectors. A call names every argument, in parameter order. A `def` is top-level. `let name = expression in expression` names a value inside a function. The name is in scope after `in`. Wrap the join in `Component(solid: join(...), expose: coords => ...)` and publish the plate's anchors again. Seat one feature per `join`. A `Solid3D` is one closed body. The patterned plate is the script to copy for this shape.

## Lessons

The language page records these lessons under "Guidance for a language model". Follow them when writing a script.

- Write a shape once and call it. A cylinder is one `Tube` and two `Disk` calls. `Tube` is the round wall. `Disk` is a cap. `CylinderAt` is that cylinder for one point of a pattern, and it publishes `at`.
- A plate is a square box: `Plate` calls `Box(width: size, depth: size, height: thickness)`. The six faces stay in `Box`. That box is centered on X and Y and stands on z = 0, so `origin` is the center and `top` is the center of the top face. The cavity example's `Box` publishes `corner` at its minimum point, and the void is seated from that corner.
- A function that is not a component uses `snake_case`, and the name says what it returns. `rectangular_pattern` returns the grid of points. `circular_pattern` returns the points of a circle. `column` and `row` count from `0`. A component uses `PascalCase`, such as `CylinderAt`.
- A size is a parameter of the part. The numbers for the file live in `parameters`. Read them with `$plate` and `$plate.size`. `pi` is the value the whole script shares.
- Map `CylinderAt` over the grid. The function receives the point and chooses `radius` and `height`, so each location can have its own cylinder. This plate uses one hole size and one pin size. `CylinderAt` publishes the point as `at`.
- `subtract_cylinders` cuts that list out of the plate. `add_cylinders` unions the pins onto the drilled plate. `map` builds the list. Each `join` then seats one cylinder, reading `plate.origin` or `plate.top` and `placed.at`.
- `integers(start: 0.0, count: 5.0)` is `[0.0, 1.0, 2.0, 3.0, 4.0]`. A list has no length. `$holes.columns` has one entry per `$holes.count`, and the square plate uses it for the rows too. `$pins.indexes` has one entry per pin. The plate uses 5 and 7.
- `|>` pipes a value into the next argument. `>>` composes two functions, runs the left one first, and binds more tightly. The plate binds `patterned_plate` as `cut_holes >> add_pins`. `items |> map` is rejected. Seat one feature per `join`. A `Solid3D` is one closed body. A call names every argument, in parameter order.
- A vector is `Vector(coords: coords, x:, y:, z:)`. `Component` passes the coordinate system into `solid: coords =>` and `expose: coords =>`. A script cannot construct that value. A helper outside those callbacks takes `coords`. `join`'s last parameter is that system and `join` ignores it, so the solid is `join(...)`. A component does not expose it. `frame.coords` does not typecheck. Inside `using`, move a point with `offset(x:, y:, z:)` and combine two vectors with `add(vector:)` or `subtract(vector:)`.

- [ParaScript language](https://parascript.lindeque.family/language.md): Rules and complete scripts for writing a model.

## Workspace

- [Workspace](https://parascript.lindeque.family/workspace): Where a person pastes a script and presses Run solver.
